title: Merge K Sorted Feeds
statement:
A user follows k creators. Each creator's posts are already sorted newest first. To build the home feed, merge them and show the newest posts first.

Write def solution(feeds, limit). feeds is a list of k feeds; each feed is a list of [timestamp, post_id] pairs sorted by timestamp, largest (newest) first. Return the post_ids of the first limit posts of the merged feed, newest first. When two posts have the same timestamp, the smaller post_id comes first (each feed already follows that rule). If there are fewer than limit posts, return them all.

Post ids are unique across all feeds.

examples.why: Timestamps in merged order: 50, 40, 35, 30, 30. Posts 2 and 5 tie at 30, so 2 goes first.
Empty feeds add nothing, and there is only one post in total.
All three posts share timestamp 7, so order by post_id: 1, 3, 8. Keep the first 2.

think.q: Each feed is already sorted. Which posts can possibly be next in the merged feed?
think.a: Only the first unused post of each feed. Anything further down a feed is older than (or ties with a larger id than) the post above it. So at any moment there are at most k candidates.

Fronts: 50 (id 1), 40 (id 4), 35 (id 7). Take id 1; feed 1's front becomes 30 (id 2). Take 4 → front 30 (id 5). Take 7, feed 3 is empty. Fronts tie at 30: take id 2, then id 5. Five taken: [1, 4, 7, 2, 5].

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Put every post in one list and sort it by (-timestamp, post_id), then slice. That costs O(N log N) for all N posts even when the feed only shows 20 of 300,000.

K-way merge with a heap. A min-heap of the k feed fronts gives the next post in O(log k). Store (-timestamp, post_id, feed, index): negating turns Python's min-heap into newest first, and post_id breaks ties.

1. Push the first post of every non-empty feed, then heapify.
  2. While the heap is not empty and you have fewer than limit ids: pop the smallest tuple, record its id.
  3. If that feed has a next post, push it.
  4. Return the ids.
No feeds, all feeds empty, or limit = 0. limit larger than the total. Ties on timestamp across feeds (and inside one feed). One feed only (the merge is just its prefix).

hints: The next post is always the front of one of the feeds. Keep only the fronts, and pick the newest each time.
heapq is a min-heap. Push (-timestamp, post_id, feed_index, position) so the newest post (and on ties the smaller id) comes out first.
After popping from feed f at position, push feeds[f][position + 1] if it exists. Stop as soon as you have limit ids.
solution:
import heapq

def solution(feeds, limit):
    # Heap of feed fronts: (-timestamp, post_id, feed index, position).
    # Smallest tuple = newest post, ties broken by smaller post_id.
    heap = []
    for f, feed in enumerate(feeds):
        if feed:
            ts, post_id = feed[0]
            heap.append((-ts, post_id, f, 0))
    heapq.heapify(heap)                    # O(k)
    merged = []
    while heap and len(merged) < limit:
        _, post_id, f, pos = heapq.heappop(heap)
        merged.append(post_id)
        if pos + 1 < len(feeds[f]):        # refill from the same feed
            ts, nxt = feeds[f][pos + 1]
            heapq.heappush(heap, (-ts, nxt, f, pos + 1))
    return merged
explain:
The heap never holds more than one post per feed. In example 1 it starts as (-50, 1), (-40, 4), (-35, 7).

  • Pop (-50, 1), push feed 1's next (-30, 2).
  • Pop (-40, 4), push (-30, 5).
  • Pop (-35, 7); feed 3 is done.
  • Pop (-30, 2) (it beats (-30, 5) on the id), push (-10, 3).
  • Pop (-30, 5). Five ids, stop.

Cost: O(k) to build the heap plus O(log k) per post shown. With 2,000 feeds and a page of 50 posts, that is about 2,000 + 50 × 11 steps, instead of sorting 200,000 posts.
complexity: O(k + limit log k) time, O(k) extra space

talk: O(k + limit log k): heapify the k fronts once, then each post shown is one pop and at most one push. Sorting everything would be O(N log N) for N total posts.
A heap because I only ever need the minimum of k candidates and the set changes by one each step. Python's heapq is a min-heap, so I negate the timestamp.
The tuple order is the tie rule: (-ts, post_id). Because post ids are unique, the comparison never reaches the feed index.
Edge cases: no feeds, empty feeds, limit = 0, limit bigger than the total, many posts with the same timestamp.
extensions: Pagination: return a cursor (the last (timestamp, post_id) shown) and fetch the next page from there without re-merging from the top.
The same post can appear in two feeds (a repost): skip ids you have already emitted with a set.
Feeds are remote and paged, 20 posts per call: refill a feed's front lazily, only when its last buffered post is popped.
Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read: when would you precompute each user's merged feed instead of merging at read time (think of a creator with 10M followers)?
